Uefa will pay clubs a total of £205m for releasing players to participate in the 2024-25 and 2026-27 Nations League tournaments, as well as both qualifying and finals matches for the 2028 Euros. The majority of that fund is reserved for clubs with players released for the Euros finals, with £120m being distributed in this instance. The remaining £89m is divided among clubs who have had players participating in either the Nations League or Euros qualifiers. Of that total, a payment of £27m is due to be released this week to clubs which had players compete in the 2024-25 Nations League. Uefa said in a statement that this will be the first payment under its Club Benefits Programme cycle. The programme means clubs are paid on a per-player, per-match basis for the Nations League tournament and Euros qualifiers, changing to per-player, per-day for the Euros tournament proper.

items.article: The supermarkets have been told ‘get their act together’ Aldi, Morrisons, and Tesco have been told to ‘get their act together’ by a litter picking group who keep having to haul supermarket trolleys out of a canal. Along a stretch of the Rochdale canal in Failsworth , litter picking group Clean Up Failsworth Canal said they regularly have to drag trolleys out of the water as part of their impressive efforts to clean up t he area . The group, which has been running for over 13 years, goes out once a month. Armed with litter pickers and dozens of bags, the team regularly find flytipped rubbish, drinks cans, and nitrous oxide or ‘laughing gas’ cannisters. On September 20, around 22 bags of rubbish had been filled and 26 cannisters were collected while 17 trolleys were fished out of the canal. The trolleys, according to the group, are increasingly becoming a problem. In some areas such as under the bridge to the town’s Tesco car park, the dumped trolleys could even mean boats struggle to get through. Sandra Ball, who represents Failsworth West for Reform UK, said: “Tesco, Aldi, and Morrisons the other end need to get their act together and get it sorted. The trolleys have always been a problem. items.article: Some foods are dangerous long before they reach a restaurant plate. Not because they are difficult to cook, but because collecting them can mean hanging from Himalayan cliffs, entering forests full of venomous insects or dealing with plants that can quietly turn an otherwise ordinary food toxic. These are seven foods whose journey from nature to the dinner table is far more dramatic than most people realise. Few foods have a harvest story as extreme as mad honey. In parts of Nepal, honey hunters collect wild honeycombs from enormous Himalayan cliff bee colonies, sometimes suspended against steep rock faces. The physical risk is only half the story. Mad honey gets its name from grayanotoxins, compounds that can enter honey when bees feed on the nectar of certain Rhododendron species. In Nepal, the honey is associated with the giant Himalayan cliff bee, Apis laboriosa. Consuming toxic batches can cause dizziness, dangerously low blood pressure, slow heart rate and abnormal heart rhythms. The remarkable part is that the danger begins with the flowers, passes through the bees and ends up in the jar. New Zealand has its own version of dangerous honey, but the story is even stranger. The culprit is tutin, a neurotoxin associated with the native tutu plant. Bees can become exposed not by collecting tutu nectar, but by collecting honeydew produced by tiny passion-vine hoppers feeding on the plant. items.text: The country that doesn't play football... yet
items.article: Nauru is the only nation to have never played an official international football match and hardly anyone there plays the game. Is that about to change? The country that doesn't play football... yet Like everywhere, the world's smallest island nation has been gripped by football fever for the past six weeks. But once Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday, almost every trace of football on Nauru stopped. Football is almost non-existent on this Pacific island. Nauru has never fielded a team in an official international match and it has just one – hard sand – pitch. While there is interest in big Premier League matches, and children wear Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo kits, any attempts to actually play football tend to be mocked, unless it's Aussie rules. But things may be slowly changing as a group of volunteers - led by British former academy player Charlie Pomroy - seek to introduce the game to what was once the world's richest nation per capita but is now heavily reliant on foreign aid and has one of the highest obesity rates in the world. A social media post from the Nauru Soccer Federation congratulating the new world champions and setting out a dream that "one day we hope to be in Spain's position" may have been fanciful, but the groundwork is real in what it says is the last country not to have had a senior international side.

items.text: ‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet?
items.article: There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare About three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger. Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day. “Before pregnancy, I used to smell my dog’s paws a lot,” says Luu. “But during pregnancy, I would throw up if I ever tried that.” At the time, Luu, 35, and Ranger had enjoyed 12 happy years together. Ranger slept in Luu’s bed. She walked him in all weather, and let him lick her face. Luu’s doctor said that her nausea was normal and simply advised her to drink more water to avoid dehydration from vomiting, but that didn’t alleviate Luu’s distress. “I was so heartbroken that I couldn’t love my dog as much as I wanted to,” says Luu, whose husband took over pet care duties. She wondered about rehoming Ranger, and was relieved when, upon delivering her firstborn, her aversion vanished. By the time of her second pregnancy, Luu was diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum . The condition is caused by hormonal shifts , much like the more familiar morning sickness. For 1%-3% of pregnant people, these shifts result in extreme nausea and disgust sensitivity that can be triggered by any number of things – in this case, pet odour.

items.article: While eating an overall healthy and balanced diet is key to preventing dementia, studies show that there are several specific foods that, when eaten too frequently, can worsen our odds. See more of our coverage in your search results. More than 6 million Americans live with dementia. With an aging population and rising cases of conditions linked to dementia, like obesity, that number is expected to double by 2060. We can’t avoid getting older — dementia’s single greatest risk factor is increasing age — but that doesn’t mean we’re powerless to stop it. We do have control over a number of factors that can lower or risk or delay dementia. Namely, our diet. While eating an overall healthy and balanced diet is key, studies show that there are several specific foods that, when eaten too frequently, can up our odds of developing dementia. As little as 25 grams of processed meat a day — think two slices of deli meat — is associated with a whopping 44% increased risk of all-cause dementia and 52% higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, a 2021 study found. Alzheimer’s is the most common cause of dementia. You don’t need to give up all red meat, though: Researchers found that eating unprocessed varieties (whole cuts, cooked from raw) was associated with lower risks.

With summer temperatures still soaring, Halloween might be the last thing on your mind. But, if spooky season is your favourite time of the year, you might want to start thinking ahead, as tickets to Thorpe Park ’s Fright Nights (one of the biggest events of the season) are cheaper when you book in advance. Returning for 2026, this year’s event marks a pretty major milestone: 25 years of scary thrills. To celebrate, the Surrey theme park has promised a brand-new scare maze, alongside reimagined shows and scare zones – although, it’s keeping further details under wraps for now. There’s also the usual lineup of rides to tackle after dark, including Hyperia, the UK’s tallest rollercoaster, and Saw The Ride, the horror-movie-themed rollercoaster. Tickets are already on sale, and booking online can save you up to £27, compared with the walk-up price. So if you’re planning a Halloween trip, it’s worth booking now, as popular dates are expected to sell out.

items.text: Why Himachal High Court quashed Bakrota land use change for hotel project
items.article: The Himachal Pradesh High Court has quashed a January 2020 permission allowing change of land use from residential to commercial in Bakrota, near Dalhousie, saying it violated the statutory Development Plan. A Division Bench of the Himachal Pradesh High Court has quashed a permission for Change of Land Use (CLU), issued in January 2020, of a residential property to commercial property in Bakrota, a small village in the close vicinity of the tourist town of Dalhousie, Chamba. The HC observed that the permission would open floodgates to the commercialisation of Bakrota In its order on Wednesday, the Bench of Chief Justice Gurmeet Singh Sandhawalia and Justice Bipin Chander Negi stated, “This permission cannot be allowed as it violates the Development Plan , which carries statutory force. Permitting this, would open the floodgates to the commercialization of Bakrota, on the ground that permission has already been granted in one case to construct a commercial building in the form of Hotels and Guest Houses which instance has also not been given.” The counsel for the petitioner, Advocate Devan Khanna, had argued that the notified Development Plan was sacrosanct and could not be ignored. He submitted that the action permitting the CLU was manifestly arbitrary, and that the impugned order was non-speaking and devoid of valid reasoning or having any element of public interest.
